claim: The African turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri) is a genetically tractable model organism for studying aging and embryonic diapause.
source: The African turquoise killifish, Nothobranchius furzeri, is a new genetically tractable model organism that has been developed for the study of aging and 'suspended animation' (embryonic diapause) (Cellerino et al., 2016; Harel and Brunet, 2015; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Platzer and Englert, 2016; Poeschla and Valenzano, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature establishing the killifish as a model organism.

claim: The African killifish has a naturally compressed lifespan of 4–6 months.
source: This fish has a naturally compressed lifespan of 4–6 months, which is 6 times shorter than the maximum lifespan of mice and 10 times shorter than zebrafish (Harel and Brunet, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The African killifish lifespan is 6 times shorter than the maximum lifespan of mice.
source: This fish has a naturally compressed lifespan of 4–6 months, which is 6 times shorter than the maximum lifespan of mice and 10 times shorter than zebrafish (Harel and Brunet, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The African killifish lifespan is 10 times shorter than zebrafish.
source: This fish has a naturally compressed lifespan of 4–6 months, which is 6 times shorter than the maximum lifespan of mice and 10 times shorter than zebrafish (Harel and Brunet, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The African killifish exhibits cognitive decline as a hallmark of aging.
source: In its short life, the African killifish exhibit hallmarks of aging, including cognitive decline (Valenzano et al., 2006a; Valenzano et al., 2006b), neurodegeneration (Bagnoli et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Terzibasi et al., 2008), fertility decline (Api et al., 2018; Zak and Reichard, 2021), cellular senescence (Valenzano et al., 2006a), impaired regeneration and wound healing (Wendler et al., 2015), defects in heart function (Ahuja et al., 2019), and an increased risk of cancer (Baumgart et al., 2015; Di Cicco et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The African killifish exhibits neurodegeneration as a hallmark of aging.
source: In its short life, the African killifish exhibit hallmarks of aging, including cognitive decline (Valenzano et al., 2006a; Valenzano et al., 2006b), neurodegeneration (Bagnoli et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Terzibasi et al., 2008), fertility decline (Api et al., 2018; Zak and Reichard, 2021), cellular senescence (Valenzano et al., 2006a), impaired regeneration and wound healing (Wendler et al., 2015), defects in heart function (Ahuja et al., 2019), and an increased risk of cancer (Baumgart et al., 2015; Di Cicco et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: In its short life, the African killifish exhibit hallmarks of aging, including cognitive decline (Valenzano et al., 2006a; Valenzano et al., 2006b), neurodegeneration (Bagnoli et al., 2022; Matsui et al., 2019; Terzibasi et al., 2008), fertility decline (Api et al., 2018; Zak and Reichard, 2021), cellular senescence (Valenzano et al., 2006a), impaired regeneration and wound healing (Wendler et al., 2015), defects in heart function (Ahuja et al., 2019), and an increased risk of cancer (Baumgart et al., 2015; Di Cicco et al., 2011).

claim: A genetic and genomic toolkit has been developed for the killifish, including sequencing of its genome.
source: A genetic and genomic toolkit has been developed for the killifish, including sequencing of its genome (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015), Tol2-based transgenesis (Hartmann and Englert, 2012; Valenzano et al., 2011), and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome-editing (Harel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A genetic and genomic toolkit has been developed for the killifish, including Tol2-based transgenesis.
source: A genetic and genomic toolkit has been developed for the killifish, including sequencing of its genome (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015), Tol2-based transgenesis (Hartmann and Englert, 2012; Valenzano et al., 2011), and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome-editing (Harel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A genetic and genomic toolkit has been developed for the killifish, including CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome-editing.
source: A genetic and genomic toolkit has been developed for the killifish, including sequencing of its genome (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015), Tol2-based transgenesis (Hartmann and Englert, 2012; Valenzano et al., 2011), and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated genome-editing (Harel et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dietary restriction impacts lifespan in a wide variety of species including worms, flies, killifish, stickleback fish, mice, rats, and monkeys.
source: A controlled feeding regimen is also critical for lifespan studies, given the impact of dietary restriction – and more generally diet – on lifespan in a wide variety of species (Fontana and Partridge, 2015; Green et al., 2022; Longo and Anderson, 2022; Mair and Dillin, 2008), including worms (Houthoofd and Vanfleteren, 2007), flies (Partridge et al., 2005), killifish (Terzibasi et al., 2009), stickleback fish (Inness and Metcalfe, 2008), mice (Bartke et al., 2001; Mitchell et al., 2019; Weindruch et al., 1986), rats (Goodrick et al., 1983; Swindell, 2012; Turturro et al., 1999), and monkeys (Colman et al., 2009; Colman et al., 2014; Mattison et al., 2017; Mattison et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In the wild, adult African turquoise killifish primarily feed upon small crustaceans and insect larvae ('bloodworms') that are present in their ephemeral ponds in Africa.
source: In the wild, adult African turquoise killifish primarily feed upon small crustaceans and insect larvae ('bloodworms') that are present in their ephemeral ponds in Africa (Polacik and Reichard, 2010; Reichard and Polačik, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Feeding with live bloodworms can introduce pathogens in the colony.
source: However, feeding with live bloodworms can introduce pathogens in the colony (Broza and Halpern, 2001; Moore et al., 2003; Rouf and Rigney, 1993), and the nutrition values of live bloodworms can vary depending on the lot and supplier (Fard et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The nutrition values of live bloodworms can vary depending on the lot and supplier.
source: However, feeding with live bloodworms can introduce pathogens in the colony (Broza and Halpern, 2001; Moore et al., 2003; Rouf and Rigney, 1993), and the nutrition values of live bloodworms can vary depending on the lot and supplier (Fard et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The automated feeder is placed on top of each animal's 2.8 L tank and drops dry food from a small feed hopper directly into the tank.
source: The automated feeder that we designed and built is placed on top of each animal's 2.8 L tank (Figure 1A) and drops dry food (e.g., Otohime fish diet) from a small feed hopper (Figure 1B) directly into the tank (which houses one individual fish).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and references to Figure 1A and 1B showing the feeder placement and design.

claim: Each rotation of the automated feeder delivers a fixed volume of food, averaging around 5 mg in mass.
source: Each rotation delivers a fixed volume of food, averaging around 5 mg in mass, and multiples of 5 mg can be programmed to increase food amount per feeding.
evidence: The claim is based on the design specifications of the automated feeder.

claim: The automated feeder operates independently of one another, allowing flexibility in feeding schedule.
source: Feedings are also fully programmable to any frequency or time of day by the user, and each feeder operates independently of one another (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), allowing flexibility in feeding schedule (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Food delivery occurred 98.1% of the time (206 actual food delivery for 210 scheduled food deliveries) for a representative feeder set to deliver 7 feedings a day for 30 days.
source: Food delivery occurred 98.1% of the time (206 actual food delivery for 210 scheduled food deliveries; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Aggregating 41 feeders for 2279 cumulative days showed that most food deliveries were fully accounted for, with only 7.89% of days deviating by one unconfirmed food delivery.
source: Overall, aggregating 41 feeders for 2279 cumulative days showed that most food deliveries were fully accounted for (Figure 2B), with only 7.89% of days deviating by one unconfirmed food delivery (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Single or multiple automated feeders were more precise, by an order of magnitude, at delivering a given amount of food compared to a group of six different individuals or a single individual measuring and delivering food.
source: Single or multiple automated feeders were more precise, by an order of magnitude, at delivering a given amount of food compared to a group of six different individuals (similar to what can be done in fish rooms to offset the workload) or a single individual measuring and delivering food (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The automated feeder can deliver up to 5 mg per unit every 10 min, or 720 mg per 12 hr period, representing a potential 20× increase over the baseline dietary regime for the day.
source: Because of its flexibility, the automated feeder can deliver up to 5 mg per unit every 10 min, or 720 mg per 12 hr period, representing a potential 20× increase over the baseline dietary regime for the day (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on the design specifications and capabilities of the automated feeder.

claim: The automated feeder can feed during the night, which would not be practical for manual feeding.
source: The automated feeder can also feed during the night, if desired, which would not be practical for manual feeding.
evidence: The claim is based on the capabilities of the automated feeder compared to manual feeding.

claim: The dietary restriction (DR) regimen led to smaller animals than the ad libitum (AL) regimen.
source: This DR regimen led to smaller (Figure 3B and C) and less fertile (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) animals than the AL regimen, consistent with what is expected under dietary restriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The dietary restriction (DR) regimen led to less fertile animals than the ad libitum (AL) regimen.
source: This DR regimen led to smaller (Figure 3B and C) and less fertile (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) animals than the AL regimen, consistent with what is expected under dietary restriction.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The average growth rate of male killifish from 1 month of age to death fed seven times a day is significantly greater than those fed three times a day in the morning.
source: The average growth rate (cm/week) of male killifish from 1 month of age to death fed either seven times a day (blue, median = 0.3726 cm/week, n = 8) is significantly greater than those fed three times a day in the morning (orange, median = 0.3 cm/week, n = 3). Each dot represents a single animal's growth averaged over its lifespan. Animals that lived longer than 4 months were not considered due to concerns with nonlinear growth rate. Significance determined by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=0.012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Killifish mating pairs fed three times a day are significantly less fertile than mating pairs fed seven times a day.
source: Killifish mating pairs (one male and one female) fed three times a day are significantly less fertile (median = 1 fertilized embryo per mating, n = 30 matings across five pairs) than mating pairs fed seven times a day (median = 4 fertilized embryos per mating, n = 30 matings across five pairs). Each dot represents the fertilized embryos collected from one pair crossing overnight, and pairs were mated from 8 weeks of age until one individual in the pair died. Significance determined by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=0.0005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3D.

claim: The average growth rate of male killifish from 1 month of age to death is significantly higher for animals fed twelve times a day than for animals fed seven times a day.
source: The average growth rate (cm/week) of male killifish from 1 month of age to death is significantly higher for animals fed twelve times a day (black, median = 0.4917 cm/week, n = 13 males) than for animals fed seven times a day (blue, median = 0.4092 cm/week, n = 5 males). Each dot represents a single animal's growth averaged over its lifespan. Animals that lived longer than 4 months were not considered due to concerns with nonlinear growth rate. Significance determined by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=0.0068).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3F.

claim: The average growth rate of female killifish from 1 month of age to death is significantly higher for animals fed twelve times a day than for animals fed seven times a day.
source: The average growth rate (cm/week) of female killifish from 1 month of age to death is significantly higher for animals fed twelve times a day (black, median = 0.4268 cm/week, n = 9 females) than for animals fed seven times a day (blue, median = 0.3425 cm/week, n = 11 females). Each dot represents a single animal's growth averaged over its lifespan. Animals that lived longer than 4 months were not considered due to concerns with nonlinear growth rate. Significance determined by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=0.012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Killifish mating pair fertility is significantly lower for animals fed twelve times a day than for animals fed seven times a day.
source: Killifish mating pair fertility is significantly lower for animals fed twelve times a day (black feeding schedule, median = 5 fertilized embryos per mating, n = 23 matings) than for animals fed seven times a day (blue feeding schedule, median = 11 fertilized embryos per mating, n = 21 matings). Each dot represents fertilized embryos collected from one pair upon crossing for 24 hr and pairs were mated from 2 months of age until one individual in the pair died. Significance determined by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=0.017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3H.

claim: Males fed the DR diet lived longer than those fed the AL diet with 16.6% median lifespan extension for cohort 1.
source: Interestingly, males fed the DR diet (orange) lived longer than those fed the AL diet (blue; 16.6% median lifespan extension for cohort 1 [Figure 4—figure supplement 1B], 22.1% median lifespan extension for cohort 2 [Figure 4B]).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Males fed the DR diet lived longer than those fed the AL diet with 22.1% median lifespan extension for cohort 2.
source: Interestingly, males fed the DR diet (orange) lived longer than those fed the AL diet (blue; 16.6% median lifespan extension for cohort 1 [Figure 4—figure supplement 1B], 22.1% median lifespan extension for cohort 2 [Figure 4B]).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Females fed the DR diet did not live significantly longer than those fed the AL diet in either cohort.
source: In contrast, females fed the DR diet did not live significantly longer than those fed the AL diet in either cohort (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Male killifish fed a DR regimen (median lifespan = 116 days, n = 21) lived significantly longer than male killifish fed an AL regimen (median lifespan = 95 days, n = 21) (p=0.0031, log-rank test).
source: Male killifish fed a DR regimen (solid orange, median lifespan = 116 days, n = 21) lived significantly longer than male killifish fed an AL regimen (solid blue, median lifespan = 95 days, n = 21) (p=0.0031, log-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Female killifish fed a DR regimen (median lifespan = 90 days, n = 25) did not live significantly longer than female killifish fed an AL regimen (median lifespan = 82.5 days, n = 24) (p=0.6798, log-rank test).
source: Female killifish fed a DR regimen (dashed orange, median lifespan = 90 days, n = 25) did not live significantly longer than female killifish fed an AL regimen (dashed blue, median lifespan = 82.5 days, n = 24) (p=0.6798, log-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4C.

claim: In DR conditions, male killifish (median lifespan = 116 days, n = 21) lived significantly longer than female killifish (median lifespan = 90 days, n = 25) (p=0.0005, log-rank test).
source: In DR conditions, male killifish (solid orange, median lifespan = 116 days, n = 21) lived significantly longer than female killifish (dashed orange, median lifespan = 90 days, n = 25) (p=0.0005, log-rank test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4E.

claim: The sex-specific effect of DR on killifish lifespan was supported using Cox proportional hazards in a factorial design, where the interaction term between sex and dietary regimen was found to be significant (p=0.045).
source: The sex-specific effect of DR on killifish lifespan was also supported using Cox proportional hazards in a factorial design (Figure 4—source data 3), where the interaction term between sex and dietary regimen was found to be significant (p=0.045).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using Cox proportional hazards model.

claim: Fitting the survival data of male killifish into a Gompertz distribution resulted in an estimated reduced slope for males in DR conditions, suggesting that this DR regimen reduces the 'rate of aging' in male killifish.
source: Furthermore, fitting the survival data of male killifish into a Gompertz distribution resulted in an estimated reduced slope for males in DR conditions. These results suggest that this DR regimen reduces the 'rate of aging' in male killifish (Figure 4F), in line with the effect of intermittent feeding on lifespan (Terzibasi et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using Gompertz distribution and reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) on the full transcriptomes showed strong separation by sex in the liver in the AL condition, and this separation was even larger in the DR condition.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) on the full transcriptomes showed strong separation by sex in the liver in the AL condition, and this separation was even larger in the DR condition (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis presented in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PCA did not reveal detectable separation by sex or diet in the brain.
source: In contrast, PCA did not reveal detectable separation by sex or diet in the brain (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis presented in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fatty acid and acetyl-CoA metabolism genes (e.g., FADS2, ACSS2, DGAT2, SCD5) were strongly downregulated in the liver in response to DR in females, but less so in males.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that fatty acid and acetyl-CoA metabolism genes (e.g., FADS2, ACSS2, DGAT2, SCD5) were strongly downregulated in the liver in response to DR in females, but less so in males (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—source data 6, Figure 5—source data 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Protein folding and ER stress response pathways (e.g., HSP90B1, DNAJB11, SDF2L1, DERL1) were strikingly upregulated in the liver in response to DR in females, but not in males.
source: Protein folding and ER stress response pathways (e.g., HSP90B1, DNAJB11, SDF2L1, DERL1) were strikingly upregulated in the liver in response to DR in females, but not in males (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Genes involved in inflammation-related pathways – positive regulators of immune responses, leukocyte activation, and cytokine-mediated signaling (e.g., CMKLR1, TBK1, BCL6) – were strongly downregulated in response to DR in the liver in males, but less so in females.
source: Finally, GSEA (but not the hypergeometric GO analysis) showed that genes involved in inflammation-related pathways – positive regulators of immune responses, leukocyte activation, and cytokine-mediated signaling (e.g., CMKLR1, TBK1, BCL6) – were strongly downregulated in response to DR in the liver in males, but less so in females (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Sex DEGs (in either AL or DR) were significantly enriched in the diet DEGs of either males or females, controlling for gene expression distribution and gene set size.
source: Interestingly, sex DEGs (in either AL or DR) were significantly enriched in the diet DEGs of either males or females, controlling for gene expression distribution and gene set size (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by enrichment analysis presented in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The average time of the first surface-bound trajectory for 13 fish was significantly shorter in the last seven trials than in the first seven trials (p=0.0005).
source: The average time of the first surface-bound trajectory for these 13 fish was significantly shorter in the last seven trials than in the first seven trials (p=0.0005) (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 6G.

claim: The percentage of successful trials in the last seven trials was significantly higher than that in the first seven trials (p=0.030).
source: The percentage of successful trials in the last seven trials was also significantly higher than that in the first seven trials (p=0.030) (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 6H.

claim: After several trials, killifish move toward the food delivery after the light turns on but before the food drops, consistent with a positive association between red light and food.
source: Thus, after several trials, killifish move toward the food delivery after the light turns on but before the food drops, consistent with a positive association between red light and food.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that fish initiate surface-bound trajectories earlier in later trials.

claim: The average velocity of young and old fish did not exhibit overt differences, suggesting that old fish could overall move.
source: We verified that the average velocity of young and old fish did not exhibit overt differences, suggesting that old fish could overall move (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Old animals (n = 8 males and females, 119–130 days of age) tended to have slightly poorer association performance compared to young ones (n = 5 males and females, 47–70 days of age).
source: Old animals (n = 8 males and females, 119–130 days of age) tended to have slightly poorer association performance compared to young ones (n = 5 males and females, 47–70 days of age) (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 6I–K.

claim: Old animals tended to have a lower 'learning index' – defined as the inverse of the first trial number needed for an animal to achieve two consecutive successes.
source: Old animals also tended to have a lower 'learning index' – defined as the inverse of the first trial number needed for an animal to achieve two consecutive successes (see 'Materials and methods') (Figure 6L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6L.

claim: At this sample size, the differences between ages were not statistically significant whether animals were binned into young and old categories or not.
source: However, at this sample size, the differences between ages were not statistically significant whether animals were binned into young and old categories (Figure 6J–L) or not (regression, Figure 6M).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in Figures 6J–M.

claim: To detect the observed effect size between young and old (Cohen's d = –0.786) at a p-value of 0.05 and power of 80%, 28 animals per age group would be needed when using learning index.
source: To detect the observed effect size between young and old (Cohen's d = –0.786) at a p-value of 0.05 and power of 80%, we estimated that 28 animals per age group would be needed when using learning index (and 27 and 132 animals per age group when using average time of first surface-bound trajectory and percentage of success, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by power analysis calculations.

claim: The automated feeders are estimated to cost 12.88 USD per feeder.
source: Additionally, our automated feeders are estimated to cost 12.88 USD per feeder (Figure 1—source data 1), so ~2000 USD for >100 tanks (including network setup and operation cost for 2 years), which is significantly less expensive than commercial systems (e.g., the Tecniplast Tritone system costs ~200,000 USD to feed approximately 240 tanks).
evidence: The claim is supported by cost estimates provided in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: The Tecniplast Tritone system costs ~200,000 USD to feed approximately 240 tanks.
source: Additionally, our automated feeders are estimated to cost 12.88 USD per feeder (Figure 1—source data 1), so ~2000 USD for >100 tanks (including network setup and operation cost for 2 years), which is significantly less expensive than commercial systems (e.g., the Tecniplast Tritone system costs ~200,000 USD to feed approximately 240 tanks).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with commercial systems.

claim: More than 100 automated feeders can operate simultaneously on the same local server.
source: We found that more than 100 automated feeders can operate simultaneously on the same local server.
evidence: The claim is based on testing of the automated feeding system.

claim: The median and maximum lifespan of the killifish in ad libitum conditions in the experiments presented in this study are shorter than some previous studies, though longer than others.
source: We note that the median and maximum lifespan of the killifish in ad libitum conditions in the experiments presented in this study are shorter than some previous studies (Hu et al., 2020), though longer than others (Terzibasi et al., 2008; Valenzano et al., 2006b).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with prior literature.

claim: Lifespan differences between sexes in response to DR are observed in other species.
source: Lifespan differences between sexes in response to DR are also observed in other species (Bronikowski et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In mice, extreme DR (40%) extends lifespan in males, but not in females.
source: In mice, extreme DR (40%) extends lifespan in males, but not in females (Mitchell et al., 2016), though milder DR leads to a greater lifespan extension in females than males (Bonkowski et al., 2006; Kane et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In mice, milder DR leads to a greater lifespan extension in females than males.
source: In mice, extreme DR (40%) extends lifespan in males, but not in females (Mitchell et al., 2016), though milder DR leads to a greater lifespan extension in females than males (Bonkowski et al., 2006; Kane et al., 2018; Mitchell et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different strains of mice exhibit more lifespan extension in response to DR in males than in females.
source: Different strains of mice exhibit more lifespan extension in response to DR in males than in females (Liao et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In flies, DR has been shown to impact lifespan differently between the sexes, with female flies enjoying the maximum lifespan benefits from DR at higher calorie levels than male flies.
source: In flies, DR has also been shown to impact lifespan differently between the sexes, with female flies enjoying the maximum lifespan benefits from DR at higher calorie levels than male flies (Magwere et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, DR is more beneficial in hermaphrodites than in males.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, DR is more beneficial in hermaphrodites than in males (Honjoh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Amount- and time-restricted DR downregulates fatty acid synthesis genes in the liver in females, more so than in males.
source: We find that amount- and time-restricted DR downregulates fatty acid synthesis genes in the liver in females, more so than in males.
evidence: The claim is based on the transcriptomic analysis presented in the study.

claim: In mice, DR downregulates lipid metabolic genes (e.g., ACYL, AACS) in females, which has been proposed to protect older animals from visceral fat accumulation and hepatic insulin resistance.

source: A dietary restriction regimen is expected to reduce growth and fertility (especially when applied early in adulthood) compared to an ad libitum feeding regimen.

source: In contrast, overfeeding has negative consequences on health, and it is expected to increase growth but to reduce fertility compared to an ad libitum regimen (Magwere et al., 2004).

claim: For 'ad libitum' (AL), fish were fed 35 mg of dry food per day, in seven feedings of 5 mg evenly spaced over 12 hr of the day, for a total of 245 mg per week.
source: For 'ad libitum' (AL, blue), we fed 35 mg of dry food per day, in seven feedings of 5 mg evenly spaced over 12 hr of the day, for a total of 245 mg per week (roughly similar to manual feeding) (Figure 3A).

source: For 'dietary restriction' (DR, orange), we fed 15 mg per day (~57% restriction), in three feedings of 5 mg over 2 hr, for a total of 105 mg per week (Figure 3A).

claim: The DR regimen is both amount- and time-restricted.
source: This DR regimen is both amount- and time-restricted (achieving amount restriction without time restriction would not be possible in current settings because of the minimum 5 mg delivery amount of automated feeder, see above).
evidence: The claim is based on the design of the DR regimen and the limitations of the automated feeder.

claim: At seven feedings of 5 mg a day (AL), animals were not overfed because they could be fed more (twelve feedings of 5 mg a day), and this extra feeding increased size but decreased fertility.
source: Importantly, at seven feedings of 5 mg a day (AL), animals were not overfed because they could be fed more (twelve feedings of 5 mg a day) (Figure 3E), and this extra feeding increased size (Figure 3F and G) but decreased fertility (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).

claim: A favorable feeding regimen, at least under these husbandry conditions, is around seven feedings per day and 35 mg of food per day for the African killifish.
source: Hence, a favorable feeding regimen, at least under these husbandry conditions, is around seven feedings per day and 35 mg of food per day for the African killifish.

source: Thus, this DR regimen (restricted in time and amount) significantly extends the lifespan of males, but not females, in the African killifish.

source: The estimated 'rate of aging' (slope) of killifish on the AL feeding regimen is 0.3388 (95% confidence interval = 0.2437–0.434) and is significantly different from the rate of aging for DR, which is 0.1457 (95% confidence interval = 0.0846–0.2069).

source: The estimated 'frailty' (intercept) for killifish on the AL feeding regimen is 0.0385 (95% confidence interval = 0.0203–0.073) compared to 0.0557 (95% confidence interval = 0.0315–0.0986) for killifish on DR (overlapping confidence intervals for intercept parameter indicate that these parameters are not significant).
